title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
authors: Xi Chen, Chunyi Zhou, Rui Zeng et al.
abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. title: PRISM: Calibrating Black-Box Judges with Counterfactual Probes
authors: Kakei Yamamoto, So Kuroki
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity m

title: ABot-ER: Unified Embodied Reasoning through Agentic Data-Model Co-Evolution
authors: Qiuyu Ding, Heng-Da Xu, Changda Xia et al.
abstract: We introduce \textbf{ABot Embodied Reasoning (ABot-ER)}, a unified embodied reasoning foundation model that breaks the tension between breadth and depth in embodied reasoning. Embodied intelligence demands the joint mastery of perception, planning, and execution, yet reconciling generality with specialization across this spectrum remains an open challenge. title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
authors: Boya Zhang, Yuanchao Ma, Jiageng Wu et al.
abstract: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this stud

title: Are We Testing Too Much? A Survey of Benchmark Compression for Efficient Evaluation of Large Language Models
authors: Guoming Ling, Yupei Lin, Zhongzhan Huang et al.
abstract: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings. title: How Reliable Are Large Language Models for Soil Organic Carbon Assessment? An Australian Benchmark
authors: Yingxuan Cheng, Tong Li, Yayong Li et al.
abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is an indicator of agricultural soil condition and carbon storage, but numerical outputs from large language models (LLMs) require validation before use in monitoring or management. We evaluated seven general-purpose LLM configurations on three direct-response tasks: estimating 0--10 cm SOC concentrations for 308 Australian paddocks under two information conditions, calculating SOC stock in 120 matched scenarios, and comparing 300 paddock pairs. References were measured

title: A Few More Tokens Ahead: Reinforcing Parallelism in Diffusion LLMs
authors: Jiahao Kuang, Yangfan Gao, Tao Gui et al.
abstract: Parallel generation is widely regarded as an inherent advantage of diffusion large language models. Yet our fixed-quota evaluation of four representative models reveals severe degradation across mathematics and code, with all scores below 15% at 16 tokens per step. Token-level probes identify local predictive potential near the observed prefix, especially in mathematical text. We propose RePara, which reinforces short consecutive token blocks through group-relative policy optimization and reduce

title: TRACESTEER: Trace Driven Activation Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Diffusion Language Models
authors: Xin Zhang, Yili Wang, Yue Tan et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We

title: SparPR: Runtime KV-Cache Recovery for Resource-Constrained LLM Inference on Consumer Hardware
authors: Jieyun Deng, Keming Hu, Yanghe Liu et al.
abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
authors: Cesare Barbera, Luca Stradiotti, Lorenzo Cascioli et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. title: From Policy Evaluation to Off-Policy Control: Provable Emergence of In-Context Q-Learning
authors: Yingjun Mo, Yajie Zhao, Fang Kong
abstract: Transformers can implement reinforcement-learning algorithms in context, yet how off-policy control emerges within Transformers remains poorly understood. We study Q-learning, a foundational model-free control algorithm that combines off-policy bootstrapping with greedy policy improvement. title: Machine--human agreement in marking undergraduate assignments is specific to model, prompt and institution
authors: Giulio Corsi, Maryam Abo-Tabik, Yael Benn et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to automate one of higher education's most resource-intensive activities: assessing student writing. Existing evaluations are typically limited to a single model, a single prompt and a single institution. Using 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities, we evaluated three frontier LLMs, individually and in ensemble, on accuracy, prompt sensitivity, error independence, generalisability and evidential basis. Agreement between human and

title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Shuwei Shen, Jincheng Tang et al.
abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. title: Virtual Head Attention
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng et al.
abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through

title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
authors: Wenbin Chen, Jiexin Wang, Guanting Wu et al.
abstract: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineeri

title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
authors: Xiaolong Xu, Hao Jiang, Bo Jiang et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. title: Perturbation, Not Provenance: Why Activation Steering Does Not Make a Robust Text Watermark
authors: Sergey Pletenev
abstract: Linear directions in the activation space of large language models causally and universally influence model behavior. This suggests that they might serve as a basis for a robust text watermark. The idea is to steer the generation along a specific semantic direction and then recover the mark by probing the activations of the re-encoded text. title: GENDIS: Gender-Related Discourse and Stance in Multilingual YouTube Comments from India, Kenya, and Nigeria
authors: Luise Koch, Manuel Tonneau, Niyati Malhotra et al.
abstract: Research on gender-related online content is often operationalized through harm-centered tasks that collapse non-harmful gender-related and unrelated content, while existing datasets remain concentrated in high-resource languages and Global North settings. title: Beyond Belief Nesting: Rethinking Higher-Order Theory of Mind in Large Language Models
authors: Shanshan You, Zhengqi Wang, Hao Liu et al.
abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order

title: CoCA: Criterion-Aware Credit Assignment for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
authors: Guangcheng Zhu, Yingfan Ma, Xing Zheng et al.
abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) evaluates responses against explicit criteria to construct rewards, offering a viable way to train large language models on open-ended tasks. However, standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards and assign uniform token advantages, leaving structured rubric supervision underutilized. Recent work seeks finer-grained guidance by treating rubrics as privileged information to derive self-distillation targets, but the resulting learn

title: Understanding Machine Taste: Aesthetic Agreement Across Foundation Models in K-pop
authors: Kaishen Wang, Yucheng Pan, Xuehao Cui et al.
abstract: As foundation models enter creative industries, understanding their aesthetic preferences becomes an important step toward AI-assisted creative decision making. In this work, we investigate how foundation models evaluate creative content and characterize their ``machine taste'' using K-pop songs and music videos as a testbed. We formulate aesthetic evaluation as a pairwise ranking problem and systematically examine pairwise inter-model agreement, group-level consensus, and cross-modal preference

title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
authors: Hardi Ashishbhai Desai, Balaji N K, Sourav Kanti Addya
abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
authors: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu et al.
abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. title: Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models
authors: Chao Li, Renhe Jiang, Chuan Xiao et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. title: Decouple to Forget: Semantic Mediation for Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
authors: Jingyue Cong, Andy Song, Yang Yu et al.
abstract: Machine unlearning for large language models seeks to remove specified knowledge while preserving general capability, yet current methods often treat an entire response as the unit of forgetting. This coarse granularity causes unnecessary utility loss when the forget target is only a small set of sensitive facts embedded within otherwise benign explanations. In this paper, we introduce Decouple to Forget (D2F), a targeted unlearning method inspired by semantic mediation that separates sensitive

title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
authors: Jiaqi Tang, Yu Wang, Yang Liu et al.
abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires f

title: Towards Green AI: Evaluating Energy Efficiency for Quantized LLM Inference
authors: Petar Basta
abstract: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation
authors: Hiroki Nishizawa, Takehiko Ohkawa, Nicola Scianca et al.
abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. title: Foundation Models for Event Prediction Across Heterogeneous Event Logs
authors: Fabian Spaeh, Sean Jaffe, Shandian Zhe et al.
abstract: Event logs are ubiquitous across real-world domains, including business processes, manufacturing workflows, healthcare, and many other operational systems. Yet event logs can differ substantially in their event semantics, label spaces, interaction patterns, and temporal scales, making it difficult to build a single foundation model that generalizes directly to previously unseen systems. title: How Safe Is ChatGPT Health Advice? Evidence from Real User Conversations in Four Global South Countries
authors: Shreyasi Roy Chowdhury, Kiran Garimella
abstract: People increasingly bring their health questions to ChatGPT, yet safety evaluations of LLM health advice rest almost entirely on clinician-authored vignettes, synthetic prompts, or simulated user profiles. The gap is widest for the Global South, where concerns about demographic bias and unsafe recommendations are well documented but have never been tested on real usage. We present, to our knowledge, the first demographically grounded safety evaluation of real-world health conversations with Chat

title: How Reliable Are System-One Decisions in Medicine? A Comparative Study of Jev, Jev-like Models, and LLMs
authors: Yanrui Du, Danyang Zhao, Sendong Zhao et al.
abstract: Jev has attracted considerable attention for its rapid, generalizable decision-making, yet its medical reliability remains under explored. To address this gap, our study compares various types of system-one decision models across 15 medical datasets comprising 8,742 instances under a unified protocol. Beyond accuracy, we assess decision stability and the ability to recognize unreliable decisions. Our results show that Jev rivals leading models on primarily text-driven tasks but is less effective

title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
authors: Mehdi Makni, Natalia Ponomareva, Rahul Mazumder
abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. title: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models
authors: Yonathan Wolanowsky, Guy Bar-Shalom, Fabrizio Frasca et al.
abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
authors: Xinyang Liao, Lingyu Li, Kaicheng Shen et al.
abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation co

title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity
authors: Yibo Wang, Senjie Jin, Yansong Ning et al.
abstract: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 co

title: AReaL-RSI: Adaptive Scaling and Coordination of Recursive Self-Improvement
authors: Wenhao Zhou, Jiajun Song, Haitao Wang et al.
abstract: Scaling recursive self-improvement requires additional computation to produce useful research progress in reaching persistent objectives. Intuitively, more researcher agents can explore more hypotheses, but early evaluation scores might misrepresent their promise, shared findings could lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures could remain confined to completed investigations. title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
authors: Petko Petkov, Giuliano Albanese, Nikolay Nikolov et al.
abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodi

title: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation
authors: Cecelia Soh, Jun Hu, Yuan Li et al.
abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. title: Rarity Determines Minimax Rates of Semantic Entropy From Weak Pairwise Judgments With a Known Channel
authors: Xiaoli Yu, Jiamiao Liu
abstract: The semantic entropy of a language model is the entropy of the meanings of its sampled answers. The meanings are never observed, and the entropy is estimated from the verdicts of a pairwise equivalence judge. Given the meanings of $n$ answers, a known channel declares each pair equivalent independently, with probability $q+Δ$ within a meaning and $q$ across meanings. title: Full-duplex Spoken Language Modeling with Discrete Diffusion
authors: Chen Chen, Pin-Jui Ku, Ankita Pasad et al.
abstract: We introduce Diffuplex, a full-duplex spoken language model based on discrete diffusion that achieves an unprecedented balance between linguistic intelligence and response efficiency. With thinking mode, Diffuplex delivers 13.0 tokens per forward pass, reaching an average of 1872 tokens per second and substantially surpassing the frontier autoregressive (AR) models in decoding speed. title: Pushback in a Haystack: Language Models Respond to Factual Errors Ambiguously and Ineffectively
authors: Li Lucy, Myra Cheng, Svenja Guhr et al.
abstract: The sycophancy of language models, or their failure to push back against faulty user input, is now widely studied. However, if LMs do push back, is sycophancy solved? We show that LMs vary in how they present pushback, and thus vary in how effectively they correct user beliefs. We introduce a phrase-level, human-validated response labeling framework to uncover fine-grained insights into how LMs push against and/or affirm false inputs. title: ARMED: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Medication Recommendation
authors: Kyungkeon Chung, Se Un Park, Hyejin Lee et al.
abstract: Medication recommendation requires jointly considering diagnoses, comorbidities, longitudinal patient history, and treatment interactions. Although recent retrieval-augmented generation approaches using language models have shown promise for clinical recommendation, most existing systems rely on fixed retrieval pipelines that cannot adapt to diverse clinical retrieval scenarios and may introduce noisy or irrelevant evidence. We propose ARMED, an adaptive clinical RAG framework that dynamically e

title: Label-Centric Knowledge Retrieval for Zero-Shot Text Classification
authors: Daoping Wu, Dong Wang, Siyu Liu et al.
abstract: Flagship large language models (LLMs) offer rich general knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but their high inference cost and latency limit their use for large-scale data labeling. We study zero-shot text classification with semantically meaningful labels and task descriptions, without task-specific labeled examples or classifier feedback. title: Improving the Evaluation of Biomedical Question Answering with Few Human Preference Signals
authors: Shakila Mahjabin Tonni, Xiang Dai, Sarvnaz Karimi et al.
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly used for biomedical Question Answering (QA). However, evaluating their effectiveness remains challenging due to the lack of reliable reference resources and the frequent misalignment between automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments. One practical question is how evaluation results should be used to guide development decisions, especially when they correlate weakly with human judgments and may even lead to different conclusions

title: The belief-action gap in language model agents
authors: Ayse Sila Okcu, Weisheng Wang, Tongmeng Xie et al.
abstract: Language model (LM) agents can fail for different reasons, requiring different explanations and interventions. We study how state beliefs, action values, and action preferences interact as LM agents reason and commit to decisions in text-rendered grid worlds. We estimate task-relevant beliefs using report-based and representation-based probes, and action values using inverse reinforcement learning. We find that task-relevant state and value information is often represented more reliably than it

title: SchemaWeaver: Accelerating On-Device Mobile Agentic AI via Schema-Guided Parallel LLM Decoding
authors: Boyuan Yang, Wei Gao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices can act as agents that call external software tools to complete complex tasks, but the major challenge of supporting on-device mobile agentic AI with LLMs is the long latency of LLM tool calling on mobile devices. In particular, the decode phase is the main contributor of such long latency, but is hard to speed up on mobile processors as it is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute power. title: Why Agentic Workflows Fail: A Taxonomy Derived from Literature and Empirical Data
authors: Xin Li, Rami Bahsoon, Tao Chen
abstract: Agentic workflows combine large language models with planning, memory, tools, execution environments, and iterative feedback. Their failures are difficult to diagnose because the same user-visible symptom may originate from model behavior, workflow orchestration, external tools, infrastructure, or their interaction. title: When Goals Leak Across Relationships: How Cached Goal Representations Shape Cross-Client Decisions
authors: Saloni Gupta, Sébastien Krier, Glenn Matlin
abstract: As LLM agents take on more autonomous roles, they may interact with multiple clients and counterparties whose goals and incentives conflict. If an agent maintains shared inference state across these interactions, information associated with one relationship may influence decisions made for another. We test OLMo-3-7B-Instruct in a controlled two-client environment with 20 market scenarios, where each client is assigned an opposing objective. title: UMCR: Universal Medical Concept Recognition through Guideline Integration and Agentic Linking
authors: Fabrice Lamarche, Amal Zouaq
abstract: Medical Concept Recognition is the task of extracting and grounding spans in medical text to entries in a standard ontology. Current methods are generally developed towards a single ontology and source text type (clinical notes, drug labels, etc.) The central challenge is therefore to build methods that adapt to any target ontology without requiring ontology-specific retraining. title: Budgeted KV-Cache Repair for Evolving Contexts
authors: Han Yu, Wenhui Zhu, Jincheng Cao et al.
abstract: Language-model agents revise their working context as information becomes obsolete, but deleting text does not erase its influence on cached computation. Later key-value (KV) states remain conditioned on the deleted content, while recomputing the entire retained suffix can be costly. We introduce budgeted KV-cache repair: recovering task performance by recomputing a user-chosen fraction of the retained suffix. title: Beyond Successful Play: Diagnosing Opponent Modeling in Large Language Models
authors: Hanbo Xie, Yue Zhao, Robert C. Wilson
abstract: Language-model agents are expected to adapt to others whose behavior changes through interaction. Yet adaptation may rely on learned behavioral patterns rather than theory of mind (ToM): the ability to infer others' mental states, including beliefs and intentions. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic framework for repeated hide-and-seek against algorithmic opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates. title: The Agent Knew: Internal States Forecast Unauthorized Actions and Stop Them, and the Lies That Follow
authors: Arya Fayyazi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
abstract: Language-model agents sometimes act beyond their authorization and then misreport what they did. title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
authors: Marcos Lima Romero, Ricardo Suyama
abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. title: MENTOR: Procedural Shielding of Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Ashwani Anand, Ivi Chatzi, Ritam Raha et al.
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficie

title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
authors: Ye Liu, Reza Averly, Avery Meyer et al.
abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to lon

title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
authors: Huihao Jing, Shaojin Chen, Wenbin Hu et al.
abstract: As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization: blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track.

title: Trace-to-Architecture: Capability Bottleneck Diagnosis for Harness Revision
authors: Wenfeng Wang, Jianrui Shi, Mingang Guo et al.
abstract: Improving an LLM agent requires knowing what to change when it fails. Similar failures can require different fixes, and resolving one problem can expose another. We introduce Trace-to-Architecture (T2A), a framework that uses execution trajectories to determine what to change in an agent's harness and when those changes apply. title: Structural Baselines Matter for Agent Failure Detection and Attribution
authors: Ramesh Arvind Naagarajan, Stefan Streif
abstract: An LLM agent using tools can fail silently. It stops before the task is done, raises no error, and answers fluently. Two kinds of monitor address this, one deciding whether a run failed and the other naming the step where failure became unavoidable. Much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from regularities that need no model. Failing runs are longer, and the step labelled decisive is usually the last. title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
authors: Min Cai, Dan Zhang, Gao Xing et al.
abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
authors: LoonSage Team, Bowei Song, Caiwei Zhao et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native,

title: Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning via Confidence-Guided Adaptive Debate
authors: Seungdong Yoa, Ye Seul Sim, Suhee Yoon et al.
abstract: Multi-agent debate has shown promise for improving the reasoning of large language models, yet recent theory suggests its benefits are highly regime-dependent. While interaction can amplify informative signals under corrective conditions, symmetric debate dynamics are neutral in expectation, often making majority voting preferable. We reconcile these views by arguing that debate is effective only when invoked at the right time and with appropriate structure. Based on this insight, we propose LAS

title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents
authors: Yutong Zhi, Jie Zhang, Xiuqi Lu et al.
abstract: As AI agents increasingly act through external tools, tool results are no longer simple outputs but execution artifacts that must remain correctly associated with the context that produced them. Yet as results persist across caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state, this association can break, causing a real and unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible execution context and lead the agent to an unsafe action. title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang et al.
abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulati

title: SLDBench v2: Active Scaling Law Discovery
authors: Lingbei Meng, Rui Huang, Zhirong Shen et al.
abstract: Scaling laws predict large-model performance from small experiments, but finding a reliable law itself requires costly experiments. SLDBench tests whether language-model agents can discover scaling laws when all experimental results are given upfront. We introduce SLDBench v2 with two extensions. First, we expand the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios spanning language-model pretraining, downstream performance, and vision-language transfer, and select 30 challenging scenarios on which a reference po

title: REVEAL: Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents from Frontier-Model Traces
authors: Yuetian Du, Meng Wang, Yucheng Wang et al.
abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profile

title: RelLedger: Relational Information Governance for LLM Agent Organizations
authors: Junxi Huang, Wenshuo Chen, Nuoxuan Li et al.
abstract: In LLM agent organizations, shared records determine which facts are available for later decisions. A sender consults interaction histories before deciding whether to report an event. A delivery gap across histories does not show whose relationship drove the choice or whether the resulting record matters downstream. We introduce RelLedger to audit these links. It holds the event, evidence, risk, and message fixed while crossing the sender's histories with the event target and an unrelated actor.

title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts
authors: Zhaoyu Fan, Bowen Han, Jincheng Ou et al.
abstract: Real-world studies (RWS) analyze routinely collected healthcare data, such as electronic health records and insurance claims, to estimate treatment effects, monitor safety, and identify risk factors outside randomized trials. Automating RWS with large language model agents is appealing but brittle: valid analyses depend on dataset-specific clinical semantics, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient/event-level units, and outcome boundaries that are often implicit in observational data.

title: Uncovering Robustness Weaknesses in LLM Agents via Persona Evolution with Task-Integrity Constraints
authors: Yutao Xie, Jingbo Yang, Guanyu Yao et al.
abstract: Interactive-agent evaluations commonly rely on standardized LLM-based user simulators that exhibit broadly cooperative behavior, potentially overlooking failures that arise under diverse but realistic user interactions. This can lead to overly optimistic estimates of agent robustness and provide limited failure signals for training agents that generalize across users. Existing approaches largely rely on predefined user behaviors, which may miss agent- or domain-specific weaknesses, while failure

title: Phantom Merge: When Your Large Language Model Agents Pick One but Tell You About Another
authors: Wangshu Zhu, Qianwen Guo, Yushun Dong
abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over multiple entities, where reliable response generation requires not only retrieving relevant evidence but also preserving its association with the correct entity. We identify Phantom Merge (PM), an entity-evidence binding failure in which an agent attributes unsupported claims to its committed entity, potentially even when the task is completed correctly. We formalize PM at the claim level and characterize its prevalence and error subtypes across four agent do

title: Large Language Model Assisted Transportation Planning through a Differentiable User Equilibrium Layer
authors: Eunseung Lee, Gyeongjun Kim, Keemin Sohn
abstract: Transportation planning has traditionally required substantial expertise in network modeling, traffic assignment, and optimization. As a result, strategic analyses such as network design, capacity expansion, and model calibration remain inaccessible to non-expert decision makers. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by enabling natural-language interaction with complex transportation planning tools. However, existing LLM-based systems primaril

title: PID-Gated Continual Prompt Adaptation Under Noisy Feedback
authors: Zhentao Xu
abstract: Deploying LLM agents in non-stationary environments requires continually revising their instructions as the task drifts, yet rewriting after every reported mistake can turn noisy feedback into persistent errors. This raises an often-overlooked scheduling question in prompt adaptation: when should feedback trigger a lasting instruction update, and at what editor-call cost? title: Scaling Multi-Agent Intelligence with Substrate-Centric Coordination
authors: Zhenting Qi, Zhuokai Zhao, Rulin Shao et al.
abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems have been shown to scale poorly, and we identify three problems: reading burden that grows with the group, useful information diluted by shared work of unknown quality, and fragility to failed agents. title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
authors: Wenqian Ye, Ziwei Guan, Zi Yang et al.
abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogen

title: When Agent Evaluation Becomes Unreliable: An Empirical Study of Oracle Failures and Configuration-Dependent Measurement in an LLM Agent Benchmark
authors: Junjie Chen
abstract: Agent evaluation harnesses are software systems that run test suites, generate inputs, and decide outcomes with test oracles. This paper audits such software for reliability defects that score tables cannot reveal. We introduce an oracle-integrity auditing approach with five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls. title: Computational Reflective Equilibrium for Agentic AI: A Rawlsian Alignment Scaffold for Governance
authors: Quanyan Zhu
abstract: The rapid deployment of agentic AI has introduced complex challenges for the ethics and governance of AI systems. Agents built on large language models act through tools on behalf of people, and each deployment case brings its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so alignment must be formed case by case. To this end, this work proposes agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), a computational reflective equilibrium framework that serves as an ethical alignment scaffold in the agen

title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
authors: Li-Ching Chen, Andrés Franco Valiente, Yuta Ishiyama et al.
abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on

title: Evaluating Temporal Reasoning in Large Language Models: Event Temporal Relation Extraction with Allen's Interval Algebra, Logical Consistency, and Relative Time in Narratives
authors: Adib Sakhawat, Fardeen Sadab, Tamjid Hasan Fahim et al.
abstract: Understanding a narrative means knowing how every event relates in time to every other, yet large language models (LLMs) are mostly tested on isolated event pairs or coarse labels. title: Soft Teacher Forcing
authors: Mohammad Fahes, Cordelia Schmid, Anurag Arnab
abstract: Soft tokens have so far been used to replace discrete chain-of-thought in latent reasoning methods. These approaches typically require multi-stage training and, in some cases, auxiliary modules, yet they still underperform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on <input, chain-of-thought, output> triples. title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
authors: Xuan Wen, Baichao Wang
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. title: AUGUstus: Autonomous Driving VLA Model with Unified Generation and Understanding
authors: Yuqi Ye, Caigao Jiang, Zhuonan Wang et al.
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. title: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
authors: Iacopo Ghinassi, Hy Nguyen Gia La, Luke Ong
abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. title: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
authors: Amir Mohammad Karimi Mamaghan, Ferdinand Kapl, Andrea Dittadi et al.
abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. title: What Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model?
authors: Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Xintong Li et al.
abstract: What could the "self" of a large language model be, if it is neither a particular word nor a single privileged layer? We propose a relational account: a functional self is an actor-centered organization of information that distinguishes the model's recorded actions from externally supplied material while content and reasoning operations change. title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
authors: Shu Gu, Matthew Youngman, Yuqin Zhao et al.
abstract: Post-route FPGA timing closure remains expert-dependent and computationally expensive. We present LATCH (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness), a two-layer framework that separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from deterministic FPGA implementation and evaluation. title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
authors: Zhipeng Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
authors: Haolin Tian, Yikang Li, Tonghan Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
authors: Zhixiong Zhuang, Jin Jia, Zhiwei Shang et al.
abstract: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. title: Rule vs.Consequence: Dissociable Internal Representations of Moral Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Eugenie Shi
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in morally and legally sensitive contexts, yet little is known about how they internally represent distinctions between moral reasoning styles. We ask whether a model's differential response to rule-framed and consequence-framed moral questions reflects distinct internal structure or merely surface lexical sensitivity. title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
authors: Jiazheng Li, Yawei Li, Junru Lu et al.
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
authors: Haoming Yang, Ke Ma, Yangbangyan Jiang et al.
abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. title: EventLens: Event-Structure Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding
authors: Guowen Zhang, Boshen Xu, Zihao Yue et al.
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong results on video question answering, yet often fail to recover the temporal structure that makes a video coherent. They may merge neighboring events, miss single-event progression, or infer implausible relations across events. We study structured temporal understanding as the ability to recover event structure from visual evidence, including event boundaries, single-event progression, and multi-event relations. title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
authors: Rishi Khare
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable

title: Query Your Way Out: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Knowledge Reasoning through Generalized Puzzle Solving
authors: Xin Cheng, Junming Yang, Ning Xu
abstract: Puzzles offer a natural testbed for Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning because they pose verifiable goals under partial information and require multi-step decisions to reach a solution. However, existing puzzle benchmarks typically focus on narrow environments with rigid mechanics and tightly constrained solution targets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Active Probing Benchmark (APB), which generalizes puzzle-solving by casting concept identification as an interactive reasoning task tha

title: ChemExplain: A Multimodal Benchmark for Explanatory Chemical Reasoning
authors: Aotian Chen, Frazier N. Baker, Reza Averly et al.
abstract: Current chemistry benchmarks primarily evaluate outcome prediction or reaction pathway generation, but rarely test whether a model can explain why an observed chemical effect occurs. We introduce ChemExplain, a benchmark of 1,180 multiple-choice chemistry questions drawn from 383 peer-reviewed papers. Each question pairs a molecular or reaction image with an observed chemical effect and four candidate explanations, each associated with a different structural feature visible in the image. Answeri

title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
authors: Huang Fei, Boyi Chen, Hao Xue et al.
abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. title: Omni-Modal LLMs Know More Than They Say
authors: Na Min An, Taekyung Kim, Jaemyung Yu et al.
abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. title: Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models
authors: Jonathan Geuter, Andrew Cheng, David Alvarez-Melis
abstract: LLM-based decision-making systems, also called System One models, have recently gained popularity, most notably through Jev (Almeida, 2026). Given a typed input state, a question, and a set of options, they return a probability for each option in a single forward pass, without text generation. title: The Format is the Filter: Scoring Format Fixes What an LLM Judge Can Express
authors: Lovedeep Gondara, Jekaterina Novikova, Sagarika Suresh et al.
abstract: When an LLM judge filters instruction-tuning data, its scoring format (binary verdict, 1--5 rating, 0--100 score, or comparison) is rarely justified or ablated. Holding the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding and selection budget fixed, we score 15,406 UltraFeedback candidates under five formats with three judges, curate, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. title: SFT Leaves a Reproducible Signature in Activation Geometry: Calibrating Post-Training Interpretability Against Run-to-Run Noise
authors: Xupeng Chen, Chenqian Le, Jiayi Cheng et al.
abstract: A model diff credits post-training with whatever separates a base checkpoint from one post-trained descendant, presuming a rerun would land close by. On the sparse co-activation graph of Qwen3-1.7B it does not: two LoRA-SFT reruns sit over half as far apart as either sits from the base. title: UZHCL_for_the_win at Touche: Encoder Fine-Tuning, Synthetic Augmentation, and an Underpowered Encoder-LLM Comparison
authors: Psychias Stylianos
abstract: Online discussions on platforms like Reddit are a productive testbed for fallacy detection: short texts, broad topical range, and the full inventory of informal fallacies. The Touche 2026 lab at CLEF formalises this as a shared task on a Reddit-derived corpus that combines fallacy detection with argument-scheme classification.
